nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.label: Sansculottes as a political pressure force
nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.meaning: Organized Parisian popular militants claim guardianship of the Republic, press economic demands, and supply the coercive strength behind political purges.
nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.stance: Their power is indispensable to the Republic yet volatile, internally divided, and capable of subordinating representative government.

nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.label: Sansculottes, moral economy, and revolutionary disillusion
nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.meaning: Sansculottes defended a moral economy, popular democracy, and suspicion of wealth and expertise that conflicted with the market liberalism and property priorities of 1789; after serving revolutionary governments, they were suppressed and left without gains.
nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.stance: In relation to the founding liberal programme, sansculotte resistance can itself be called anti-revolutionary, despite its familiar status as the paradigm of popular revolution.

nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.label: Revolutionary calendar and Year I
nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.meaning: The later revolutionary calendar dated Year I from the Republic's foundation in September 1792, formalizing the break with monarchy.
nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.stance: The calendar is retrospective institutionalization of the republican rupture, not an event that caused the September declaration.

nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.label: Republican calendar: secularization of public time
nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.meaning: The October 1793 calendar that dated years from the Republic, renamed months seasonally, replaced seven-day weeks with décades, and displaced Sundays.
nonidentical_chapter_formulation_fields.stance: Although not itself identical with dechristianization, its timing encouraged representatives to intensify the attack on Christian practice.
